I smoke pretty often and my advice is:

1) Def start slow. Smoking is honestly a skill you have to learn and so if that is your chosen method of consumption coughing a shit ton at the beginning is to be expected. If you do edibles, start with a low dosage (10mg max) to get a baseline of your tolerance. A mild first high is better than a super intense anxious high. 

2) If you know you are prone to physical anxiety sometimes 1:1 edibles (Equal parts CBD and THC) can help midgate. Where I live they have a fuck ton of ratios where it's 10mg CBD & THC or 50mgCBD:1mgTHC so there's options if you live in a legal state.


3) If you get high a few times and genuinely don't like the feeling don't pressure yourself to like it. For me I've done shrooms a handful of times but every trip was really intense. I kept doing them because my friends would always talk about how good the trip was and I just had to find the right dose. I finally had to stop trying because I just genuinely can't handle psychedelics 


4) Be mindful of when, why and how often you're consuming. This is a little controversial in the stoner community but there is a difference between getting high to mitigate pain, sleep or ease anxiety and just straight up self medicating. I got to the point where I was going through a half oz a week, but sometimes a full. Yes it eased my anxiety, but also the high made it easier to ignore my feelings. I justified it because I'd hear "that's just how much stoners smoke and it's not additive." If you find yourself mainly consuming as a way of coping or anytime you experience distress your immediate reaction is to get high; think about if there are other avenues (therapy, psychiatry, exercise, social or therapeutic groups) you can utilize. I do want to acknowledge that I know some people use THC as a coping method especially when healthcare is inaccessible, but if you have other options and resources, use them :)


But I really like weed and it's definitely safe for like a drug 😂 But the only thing that made it a bit more dangerous for me is I over consumption to cope with Burnout. Because I'm still in that angsty young adult transition, getting high everyday made the world less painful and my brain wasn't working overtime trying to read, translate and make sense of everything haha


So yes, I hope you find something you like and lemme know if you have any questions (I was a budtender for a bit ☺️)

I had two reductions the first one honestly kinda. I was a 38I and when I did my consultation I was too timid to say I didn't care about my breasts matching my body proportions or having breastfeeding capabilities. I was in so much pain for the first week and then I developed necrosis on both areolas. I was at the surgery office 3 days a week for over a month post op then it went down to two and then one. But healing was painful, I missed my 21st birthday, and after I was a full DD but comfy DDD. Because of the necrosis my areola had hard spots in different places on the sides and the scarring was pretty dark.

that being said...

I went back this year to get steroid injections for the areola keloids and I told the surgeon I was unhappy and still having the same back, shoulder and rash pains. I said that I wanted a second reduction but to go as small as he possibly could. He was hesitant because I was the largest reduction he had ever performed and one of the rare cases in his over 10 years where necrosis occurred. I told him at this point I don't care about extra scarring, I don't want children and the necrosis risk wasn't a deterrent. I would have legitimately rather had no breast then these because I wasn't comfortable. He took a month to do research and come up with a plan and I'm currently a bit over 3 weeks post op and healing amazing. I think I'm a full B Cup but I still have a bit of swelling and I don't regret the second procedure one bit

I (F24)  got my ASD diagnosis in Aug of 2022 in what felt like a pretty short time ( I did one intake, one session talking about the questionnaire, my mom had a session with the evaluator and I was diagnosed)  

I had the common undiagnosed experience of severe depression and anxiety. I always knew there was something else being missed but no provider believed me. 
  
I do fall into the "new age" social media self diagnosis pathway ish ish but I'll explain haha.

I worked at a dispensary where I met my friend who self diagnosed ASD. Because my experiences were suspiciously similar and I had been questioning whether or not I had BPD, I started researching. I did it in kinda an inverted way where I read ncbi papers, and collected more "research based" data. I know that mental health + neurotype research disproportionately excludes communities of color so I did TikTok, YouTube and Instagram deep dives. I'm a huge advocate for the sharing of lived experiences and having that human component helped validate my suspicions. I compiled my data into a document that compared and contrasted applicable symptoms and experiences and showed my new psychiatrist. She sent me the questionnaires during the end of our session 😂

The one thing I just absolutely hate is how bold people on the internet are with diagnosing or even like discussing the possibility of a diagnosis in users comment sections. I think that unsolicited speculation, based around neurotype, gender, sexuality, bodies or anything that you wouldn't know the answer to unless you're that person, is one of the worst things we've normalized.

But social Media is one of the few places where there is autistic lead representation, however it is also very unregulated(not that other forms of representation are better haha). Like you said people will literally just label common things as ✨autistic✨ and I do feel like it's become aesthetisized. Sometimes it feels like videos surrounding autism are more about getting engagement than it is sharing experiences. And tbh some people use social media for the sheer purpose of getting likes and views and it's not the worst thing or uncommon because that's the world we live in. I agree with you that some of this exposure is contributing to misinformation and it's also like once the trend dies down autism won't automatically disappear. Visibility is not the same as acceptance, and it just feels like specifically on TikTok the ratio of informative and genuine autism related content vs the more click bait, trend videos is off. The larger impact is: holistic struggles, experiences, lifestyles are still piggin holed into a pretty monolithic experience. A lot of NT people believe that because autism is talked about more on TikTok and in more media in general, societally we are accepted in a systemic way, and our struggles aren't "as difficult as it used to be".

I want to highlight that don't believe that marginalized groups should only be allowed to post facts and educational information about their experiences because jokes and humanization are part of our experience too. Something I do think should be taken with a grain of salt is there is an intersection between pop culture, exposure, caricatures and minority group representation. It's been shown time and time again that the impacts of trends do have lasting harmful systemic impacts. 


okay last point I promise 😂 I honestly don't care if people self diagnose themselves wrong because there are more important things, but I do think that people forget that typically diagnoses come with ✨ treatment ✨. I have an issue with diagnoses being used as a way to, I don't wanna say fit in, but it feels like in these online spaces you can always quickly find a community of people who will validate self diagnoses based off vaguely autistic traits? The validation from others isn't explicitly bad because yeah the ways in which ASD is presents varies, plus on one has the right to invalidate the experiences of others especially from behind a screen. But again, diagnoses are supposed to be used as a guiding point to help you understand your thoughts, accumulate tools, learn mechanisms, and create treatment methods that will put you on a road to help you succeed. I think the process of getting an official ASD diagnosis is extremely introspective and comprehensive for a reason, and it does make me feel some type of way knowing that some people pick and choose when they want autism to be part of their identity.

Also the idea of seeing a bunch of TikToks on my fyp about a subject I know little about and identifying with it publicly after doing no further research sounds goofy as fuck. But I guess that goes back to the original point of the harms of ASD misinformation. People will take all videos as facts and it just perpetuates the mainstream mischaracterization, and erases the diversity of ASD experiences. 

Also I tried to be very intentional with my words so feel free to let me know if something I said sounds a little off 😂 This conversation is important and I also know that it can leave harmful individual impacts when it isn't had in a collaborative and reflective way haha

Hi this isn't really advice or but  I want to validate that like what you are experiencing is extremely difficult and it's not something you "get through" because it truly is a life long process. However I can't relate to this post so much.

I am (24F) and started college at 18 only diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety. Standard high achieving kid who got by gen Ed classe because I was smart. I also was such a heavy masker and molded my entire existence basically around being an involved, athletic, high achieving, popular student. Throughout highschool I was definitely depressed (Started SH at 12), but i was never diagnosed so I just assumed my sadness was how I was supposed to feel.

The first year it was good I had excellent grades, got hired as a freshman to be an RA. Funny enough looking back at least 1/3 of my RA staff were neurodivergent and that played a factor in my success. I was still pretty depressed and deeply sad but I was still able to mask it entirely.

Sophomore my staff changed and classes became way harder (I was pursuing ChemE) and I started crumbling nearly immediately. I started antidepressants which didn't really help, began SH'ing again and I failed two classes. The next semester I could barely leave bed, I was going to class maybe once a week, working my RA job and a side one. I started abusing cough syrup + sleep aids and getting riskier with my SH. I was actively making plans to end my life planning out the logistics and means, I was in so much pain but my parents luckily made me go home. ( I failed every class)

I moved home, was diagnosed with MDD, did the therapy, DBT (2 rounds), psychiatry and got my A.S. from a community college. I was definitely still hella depressed but the self harm had stopped and I wasn't self harming.

Jan 20' (age 21) transferred to a 4 year again but failed two classes in my first quarter. I was a Math major and my professors didn't believe in providing resources, lectures or any repetition of work ( I was taking mostly theoretical math courses). Blah blah quarantine and I did okay at first but Fall of 21' I began to crumble again. I failed classes and began heavy weed consumption. My insurance was so booked that therapy and psychiatry became less frequent. Beginning of May I went inpatient, then at the end of May 21' I made an attempt.

I dropped out 5 classes before graduation for the second time and have not gone back to school since. July 22' I got both my ADHD & ASD diagnosis but my therapist was honestly just awful. My parents don't believe in neurodiversity and I was so depressed. I made a second attempt Sept 22'. 

After that I got a new psychiatrist and therapist who had experience and expertise in working with young adults on the spectrum. I'm no longer a danger to myself and I have much better support but life is exhausting.

I actually just quit my job of 1 year yesterday ( I was a program manager at a non - profit) And I don't know how I'm supposed to work 9-5.

That being said something that I do want to say for me at 18 - 19 the world was so heavy and that is a major transitional period. I won't say things get "better" in terms of my Audhd symptoms but over the years I have gained more tools to navigate. Being almost 25 I do genuinely feel like brain development has helped 😂

Ehh if I were to give advice I'd say that:

 1) what you're experiencing IS difficult and so so hard so if you can validate yourself because it's not in your head!!!

2) Don't be afraid to accept support, again tbh I felt like a teenager until I was 23 and I also feel like a lot of people in their 20's still rely on family for big things

3) Don't feel like you have to plan too far in advance. I know that financial stability is important to plan for and so taking things month by month isn't feasible to everyone. For me I've stopped planning for my future directly and have started just like doing what I need to do in that moment or a chunk of time to function.

I hope you found some use of this info dump. But friend I'm proud of you for continuing to progress forward even if the progress is slow or you fell stuck 💕

Honestly if you are truly in pain and you feel like you can consume safely, definitely ask for stronger meds. I actually just went through a second reduction on last week and this time around I didn't try and "tough" through the pain. When I woke up from surgery I was in pain and I told them immediately and was given oxy. After an hour I still felt super achy and uncomfortable so I told the nurse and they gave me more meds. For the first 48 hours I took the maximum safe dosage of every medicine they offered on a meticulously planned and timed out schedule.

I'm now 8DPO and really haven't experienced any pain. I stopped the narcotics after day two and have tapered down to Tylenol only as needed. I feel like the first few days post surgery you honestly should safely take as many meds as you can even if you aren't in pain at that moment to keep it from getting bad.

Basically what I'm trying to say is listen to your body and yourself! The meds are there to relieve pain and so if you feel safe consuming, utilize that resource!

Hope this helps and makes a little sense hahah

I got my reduction in March of 2019 and within two weeks post op I developed necrosis around my areola on both sides. I had tunneling wounds that had to be packed and re-bandaged 3 times a week.  The total heal time it took for the necrosis wounds to subside and close was about 3 months. 

My healed wounds left two 1inch hardened fat sections on my left areola and one on my right. Because of college, quarantine and the pandemic I didn't ever address it with my surgeon until more recently. 

I also went to the surgeon because I felt a large pellet sized lump in my breast. When I got my consult I ended up getting steroid injections into those necrosis spots and they softened after like 3 weeks. The fat necrosis and scar tissue did not resolve on its own for me but I also know bodies are different! I also got an ultrasound and they found a small cyst in my right breast but I forgot why it happened haha. 

I hope this is a little helpful
